mcqs.q: Dental amalgam has been the primary direct restorative material for:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam has been the primary direct restorative material for more than 100 years, though its use is now declining.

mcqs.q: The decline in amalgam use is attributed in part to:
opts: Tooth-coloured composites and the minimally invasive nature of their preparations
mcqs.explain: Interest in tooth-coloured composite resins and their more minimally invasive preparations has reduced amalgam use.

mcqs.q: Success of an amalgam restoration depends on:
opts: Proper cavity preparation AND proper manipulation of the amalgam
mcqs.explain: Both proper cavity-preparation principles and proper manipulation of the amalgam are needed for a successful restoration.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of amalgam manipulation steps?
opts: Select alloy → proportion → triturate → mull → condense → burnish → carve → finish/polish
mcqs.explain: The sequence is: selection of alloy, proportioning, trituration, mulling, condensation, burnishing, carving, and finishing/polishing.

mcqs.q: Which factor affects the selection of an amalgam alloy?
opts: Particle size/shape, copper content, and zinc presence
mcqs.explain: Alloy selection considers particle size/shape, low vs high copper content, and the presence/absence of zinc.

mcqs.q: More than 90% of amalgam alloys used today are:
mcqs.explain: Over 90% of amalgams now used are high-copper alloys.

mcqs.q: The KEY advantage of high-copper amalgam is the elimination of:
mcqs.explain: High-copper amalgams have no gamma-2 phase, which gives high early strength, low creep, and good corrosion/marginal-fracture resistance.

mcqs.q: An advantage of eliminating the gamma-2 phase is:
opts: Low creep and good corrosion/marginal-fracture resistance
mcqs.explain: Without gamma-2, high-copper amalgam has high early strength, low creep, and good corrosion and marginal-fracture resistance.

mcqs.q: Zinc-containing alloys (>0.01% Zn) can cause:
opts: Excess (delayed) dimensional change if contaminated by moisture
mcqs.explain: Zinc-containing alloys show excess (delayed) expansion if contaminated by moisture during condensation.

mcqs.q: Compared with lathe-cut particles, spherical alloy particles are:
mcqs.explain: Spherical particles are smoother with a lower surface/volume ratio; lathe-cut particles are rough and irregular.

mcqs.q: The recommended mercury/alloy ratio for LATHE-CUT alloys is about:
mcqs.explain: Lathe-cut alloys need ~1:1 (≈50% mercury); spherical alloys need less (~42%) due to their lower surface/volume ratio.

mcqs.q: Spherical alloys require less mercury (≈42%) because they:
mcqs.explain: Spherical particles have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, so they need less mercury to wet the surfaces.

mcqs.q: Using TOO LITTLE mercury results in:
opts: A dry mix with reduced strength and corrosion resistance
mcqs.explain: Too little mercury gives a dry mix that impairs strength and reduces corrosion resistance; too much causes setting expansion.

mcqs.q: Using EXCESS mercury results in:
opts: No mercury in the final restoration
mcqs.explain: Excess mercury increases setting expansion (and weakens the restoration), so mercury should be controlled and excess expressed during condensation.

mcqs.q: Trituration of pre-proportioned capsules is done in a/an:
mcqs.explain: Pre-proportioned capsules (alloy and mercury separated by a septum) are triturated in an amalgamator.

mcqs.q: Condensation of amalgam is done to:
opts: Adapt it to the cavity walls and bring excess mercury to the surface
mcqs.explain: Condensation packs the amalgam, adapting it to the walls and bringing the mercury-rich layer to the surface for removal.

mcqs.q: Burnishing the amalgam helps to:
opts: Smooth the surface and remove the mercury-rich layer
mcqs.explain: Burnishing smooths the surface and removes the mercury-rich surface layer, improving the margins.

mcqs.q: Carving the amalgam is performed to:
mcqs.explain: Carving reproduces the occlusal anatomy and proper occlusion before the amalgam fully sets.

mcqs.q: Finishing and polishing of amalgam is best delayed for about:
opts: 24 hours (after the amalgam has fully set)
mcqs.explain: Finishing/polishing is delayed ~24 hours until the amalgam has fully set, improving smoothness and corrosion resistance.

mcqs.q: Mercury toxicity in the dental office is mainly due to:
mcqs.explain: The main hazard is inhalation of mercury vapour, so handling and ventilation precautions are essential.

mcqs.q: Which is a measure to prevent mercury hazard?
opts: No-touch technique, capsules, good ventilation and storing scrap under water
mcqs.explain: Mercury hygiene includes a no-touch technique, pre-capsulated amalgam, good ventilation, storing scrap under water/fixer, avoiding heat, and proper waste disposal.

mcqs.q: Mulling of amalgam refers to:
opts: Homogenising the triturated mass into a cohesive mix
mcqs.explain: Mulling homogenises the freshly triturated amalgam into a smooth, cohesive mass before condensation.
